title: Form submission lifecycle and successful controls
learningObjectives: Explain form submission lifecycle and successful controls and build forms with appropriate native HTML behaviour.

understand.concept: A form submission starts when the user submits a form or a submitter triggers submission. The browser constructs the form data set from successful controls: controls generally need a name, must not be disabled, and must meet the relevant successful-control rules. The submitter can contribute its own name and value.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding submission explains why some visible controls are absent from the submitted data. Native submission also includes validation and submitter behaviour that custom JavaScript must preserve deliberately.
understand.analogy: A form submission is like preparing an envelope: only eligible, labelled fields are placed inside it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; actual form submission and validation follow HTML algorithms and browser behaviour.

explain.narrative: The named text field, checked checkbox, and activated submit button can contribute name/value pairs. Unchecked and disabled controls are not submitted as successful controls.

examples.code: <form action='/demo' method='get'><label>Name <input name='name' value='Asha'></label><label><input type='checkbox' name='updates' value='yes' checked> Receive updates</label><button name='action' value='save'>Save</button></form>
examples.explanation: The named text field, checked checkbox, and activated submit button can contribute name/value pairs. Unchecked and disabled controls are not submitted as successful controls.
examples.expectedOutput: A browser-rendered form demonstrating the HTML form behaviour described.

practise.guidedTask: Add a disabled input, an unnamed input, and an unchecked checkbox. Predict which controls are included when the form is submitted.
practise.independentTask: Build an accessible form using appropriate input types, names, labels, and constraints. Inspect the submitted FormData and explain which controls are successful.
hints: Give every user-facing control a visible label.
Do not trust hidden fields or client-side validation for security.
Test keyboard and mobile input behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which attribute is generally required for a control to contribute a name/value pair?
questions.explanation: Successful controls generally need a name attribute to be included in form data.

questions.prompt: What is a good form-design principle?
options: Use semantic controls, visible labels, and server-side validation
questions.answer: Use semantic controls, visible labels, and server-side validation
questions.explanation: Accessible forms use appropriate controls and labels, while security validation belongs on the server.
